Re-examining the application of the Theory of Planned Behavior model in Physical Education:

Supplementing the motivational modification model

## Abstract

The Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) is widely used to explain students’ physical activity

participation in physical education. To examine whether motivation adds explanatory value to TPB, this

meta-analysis synthesized 60 independent studies (N = 38,596; 496 effect sizes) and tested a motivation-

extended TPB model using two-stage meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM). The model

retained the core TPB pathways (ATT, SN, and PBC → BI → PB), added internal TPB paths (SN →

ATT, SN → PBC, and PBC → ATT), and included broad physical activity motivation (PAM) as an

antecedent of TPB constructs and PB. All hypothesized paths were statistically significant. The

motivation-extended model showed better overall fit than the base and internally extended TPB models.

PAM was positively associated with ATT, SN, PBC, BI, and PB, and the conventional TPB paths also

remained significant. However, heterogeneity across primary studies was high for many pooled

relationships, indicating that the observed associations should be interpreted as average tendencies rather

than fixed effects. Because the included studies were observational and largely cross-sectional, the

findings support theoretically specified pathways but do not establish causal effects or intervention

effectiveness. Overall, the results suggest that incorporating motivation may broaden the explanatory

scope of TPB in physical education and can inform future longitudinal and experimental research.

Keywords: Theory of Planned Behavior; Physical activity motivation; Physical education; Meta-

analytic structural equation modeling

## 1. Introduction

Regular exercise is beneficial for long-term health and can help prevent a range of physical and

psychological problems. However, students’ participation in physical activity remains insufficient in

many educational settings (Diehl et al., 2018). Both K-12 education and higher education are important

stages for the development of health-related habits, and exercise patterns formed during these periods

may influence not only students’ current physical fitness but also their long-term lifestyle and health

trajectories (Spruijtenburg et al., 2024). School-based physical education in primary and secondary

education, extracurricular sport participation during adolescence, and more autonomous exercise patterns

in university settings may all contribute to the development of lifelong physical activity habits(Coimbra

et al., 2021). For this reason, a clearer understanding of the factors associated with students’ physical

activity participation is important for explaining and predicting participation-related behavior(Yao et al.,

2024). Identifying a theoretically robust and practically interpretable model is therefore an important step

in understanding how students’ participation in physical activity can be supported in educational

contexts(Liao et al., 2022).

Among the theoretical models used to explain health-related and sport-related behavior, the Theory

of Planned Behavior (TPB) has been widely applied because of its relatively clear structure and strong

explanatory tradition (Bae et al., 2020). TPB originated from the Theory of Reasoned Action and was

further developed by Ajzen (1991), who proposed that attitude (ATT), subjective norms (SN), and

perceived behavioral control (PBC) jointly shape behavioral intention (BI), which in turn is associated

with behavior. In physical education research, TPB provides a useful framework for explaining why

students are willing to participate in physical activity and whether they are likely to translate that

intention into actual participation behavior (PB). Existing studies have shown that students’ evaluations

of physical activity, their perceptions of expectations from teachers and peers, and their beliefs about

their own capability and opportunity to participate are all associated with BI and PB  (Deng et al., 2024;

Rullestad et al., 2021). Nevertheless, as research has accumulated across different educational and social

contexts, the limits of the traditional TPB framework have become more visible.

One important limitation is that the traditional TPB model places stronger emphasis on proximal

social-cognitive beliefs than on the motivational processes that may energize participation in the first

place. In physical education, physical activity motivation (PAM) is likely to be closely related to whether

students value participation, persist in activity, and maintain involvement over time(Kelso et al., 2020;

Macali et al., 2025). Self-determination theory suggests that different forms of motivation may be

associated with different patterns of persistence, engagement, and self-regulation(Vallerand, 2000). In

sport and exercise contexts, motivation-related constructs such as interest, challenge, self-expression,

and social connection have been linked with students’ attendance, extracurricular participation frequency,

and commitment to training (Vallerand & Ratelle, 2002). Some studies have also pointed out that the

higher the level of motivation, the more frequent their self-regulatory behaviors (such as active practice,

goal setting, and self-feedback), which in turn enhances the efficiency of the transformation from BI to

PB (Dishman et al., 2015). These findings suggest that motivation may represent an important

explanatory component that is not fully captured in the traditional TPB model.

A further reason to consider PAM more explicitly is that physical education participation is

embedded in real teaching and learning environments. Students’ motivation may be related not only to

participation itself, but also to how they experience classroom climate, teacher support, and engagement

in activity-based learning contexts (Schmidt et al., 2018). This issue may be especially relevant in

contemporary PE environments that increasingly incorporate digital, gamified, or technology-enhanced

elements. In such settings, instructional innovations may be more effective when students are already

willing to engage with physical activity, whereas low motivation may be associated with weak

participation even when facilities or instructional tools are available (Antunes et al., 2024; Sun et al.,

2025). Accordingly, integrating PAM into TPB may help provide a more complete account of how

motivational and social-cognitive factors jointly relate to students’ BI and PB in physical education.

Based on these considerations, the present study re-examines TPB in the context of physical education

by comparing the traditional TPB model, an internally extended TPB model, and a motivation-extended

TPB model. In addition to testing the pooled structural relationships among PAM, ATT, SN, PBC, BI,

and PB, this study also examines whether selected paths vary across educational stages and regional

economic contexts. In doing so, the study aims to provide a more integrated understanding of the

association patterns underlying students’ physical activity participation in educational settings.

## 2. Literature review and hypotheses development

### 2.1 TPB model

The theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) was first proposed by Fishbein and Ajzen (1977) based on

the Theory of Reasoned Action (TRA). It was further expanded by Ajzen (1991), who incorporated PBC

into the model and constructed a comprehensive theoretical framework in which ATT, SN, and PBC

jointly influence BI and ultimately transform it into PB. ATT refers to the overall positive and negative

evaluation and emotional tendency of an individual's participation in a particular sports activity, including

expectations and value judgments on the results of the activity (such as physical fitness improvement,

health improvement, teamwork, etc.) (Ohashi et al., 2023). When students believe that the activity can

bring positive consequences, the more positive their attitude is, the stronger their BI is (Bechler et al.,

2021). SN refers to the social expectations and pressures that individuals perceive from important

reference groups, such as teachers, peers, and parents, regarding their participation in sports activities.

This includes the belief that "others want me to do" or "don't want me to do" and their compliance

motivation (Howie et al., 2020). In physical education classes, the encouragement and evaluation of

teachers and peers will significantly enhance students' BI (Ruzek et al., 2016). PBC refers to an

individual's sense of control and confidence in the ability, resources, and external conditions (such as

venues, equipment, time arrangements, etc.) required to complete a particular sports activity (Lidong et

al., 2025). When students believe that they have sufficient skills and resources, their perceived behavioral

control level is higher, and it is easier to convert BI into actual action (Lidong et al., 2025) BI refers to

an individual's subjective motivation and plan for participating in sports activities at a specific time and

situation (Feil et al., 2023). BI is regarded as the most direct behavioral predictor, and its strength

determines the possibility of actual participation (Zhang et al., 2022). Physical activity participation

behavior (PB) refers to the performance of an individual in actual action during physical education and

extracurricular exercise, which can be measured by objective or self-reported indicators such as

frequency of class participation, duration of extracurricular exercise, exercise intensity, and project

diversity (Mayorga-Vega et al., 2018). Studies have shown that there is a significant positive correlation

between behavioral intention and actual sports behavior ("intention → behavior" conversion effect)

(Lidong et al., 2025).

In the context of physical education, TPB provides a clear theoretical framework for understanding

and predicting students' participation in sports activities. Whether students participate in and persist in a

particular sports activity depends on the BI formed by their overall evaluation of the activity, perceived

social expectations, and self-control ability, and is ultimately converted into PB (Bae et al., 2020).

Specifically, when students believe that a particular sport can effectively improve physical fitness,

promote physical and mental health, and enhance teamwork or social skills, they will have a positive

attitude toward the project (Nie, 2024). At the same time, the teacher's demonstration and encouragement,

peer support and evaluation, and parents' expectations will build a kind of SN pressure, making students

perceive that "important others" want them to participate in sports activities (Spruijtenburg et al., 2025).

Driven by this attitude and subjective norms, students also need to evaluate whether they have sufficient

physical reserves, venue resources, time arrangements, and related skills to judge their sense of control

or mastery over participating in the activity (Ouyang et al., 2020). When students believe they can

flexibly allocate their spare time, master the necessary sports skills, and have access to stable sports

venues and equipment, their perceived behavioral control level increases, thereby enhancing the

likelihood of putting their intentions into practice (Ator & Ortizo, 2024). The above three factors - ATT,

SN, and PBC - are intertwined and mutually reinforced in the individual's mind and ultimately contribute

to the formation of BI; that is, students subjectively "intend" or "plan" to participate in the sport. A

substantial amount of research evidence indicates that BI is the most significant direct predictor, which

largely determines whether PB occurs (Feil et al., 2023). For example, if a college student strongly agrees

that football training can bring both physical fitness and teamwork benefits and his coach and teammates

consistently give him affirmation. He believes that he has sufficient physical conditions and technical

level. He will clearly show a strong BI and eventually actively attend and participate in weekly physical

education classes and after-school training. On the contrary, if any of the above links is weak - such as

insufficient understanding of the value of sports, lack of peer support, or finding it difficult to make time

- it may weaken their BI and even lead to the intention formed being unable to be transformed into actual

behavior (Cheval et al., 2024).

### 2.2 The extended TPB model

The TPB model assumes that the three core variables that determine BI (PBC, ATT, and SN) are

independent of each other. This is unrealistic in practice, as PBC will inevitably affect ATT and SN, and

the high correlation between these constructs supports this, so it is often discussed in the literature as a

common methodological bias (Leong et al., 2023). Exploring these potential new connections between

TPB constructs is crucial because it can provide new theoretical contributions to scholars and theorists

and deepen the understanding of TPB. Subjective norm is an important construct of TPB, which

represents the opinions of the outside world on individual behavior and its subsequent impact (Ajzen,

1991). Over the years, research has strengthened the hypothesis that SN affects PBC; that is, this

construct is one of the influencing factors of sustainable sports participation (Ordiñana-Bellver et al.,

2024). This suggests that if students believe their environment can support their decision to participate

in sustainable sports, they will be more willing to engage in this behavior. For ATT, many researchers

have found that both SN and PBC can directly affect ATT, and this is also the case in sports (Chi, 2024).

On this basis, the following hypotheses are proposed:

H6: Subjective norm is positively associated with perceived behavioral control.

H7: Subjective norm is positively associated with attitude.

H8: Perceived behavioral control is positively associated with attitude.

### 2.3 Motivation-extended TPB model

The theory of planned behavior (TPB) explains how attitudes (ATT), subjective norms (SN), and

perceived behavioral control (PBC) are associated with behavioral intention (BI) and, ultimately,

physical activity participation behavior (PB). However, TPB pays less attention to why students are

energized to participate in the first place and how motivational processes may shape the proximal social-

cognitive predictors within the model(Chan et al., 2020). Self-determination theory (SDT) helps address

this limitation by emphasizing that motivation varies in quality and is closely related to persistence,

engagement, and behavioral self-regulation (Ryan & Deci, 2000). In this sense, integrating motivation

into TPB does not “correct” TPB, but extends it by incorporating a motivational basis for students’

participation-related cognitions and intentions(Alam et al., 2019). Meta-analytic evidence further

suggests that self-determined motivation is associated with the proximal predictors of intention and

behavior proposed in TPB(Hagger & Chatzisarantis, 2009). In physical education (PE), this implies that

motivation may be meaningfully associated with students’ attitudes, perceived control, intentions, and

participation.

Importantly, the present study does not treat physical activity motivation (PAM) as synonymous

with a single SDT regulation type. SDT distinguishes autonomous and controlled forms of motivation,

and this qualitative distinction is theoretically important. However, the primary studies included in this

meta-analysis reported different motivation indicators, including intrinsic motivation, extrinsic

motivation, autonomous motivation, and composite or total motivation scores derived from instruments

such as the Sports Motivation Scale (SMS) and the Sport Motivation Questionnaire (SMQ). To construct

a common MASEM matrix across studies, PAM was therefore coded as a broad construct reflecting the

overall level of motivation toward PE or physical activity participation rather than a single motivational

subtype. Accordingly, the findings should be interpreted as broad motivation-related associations, not as

effects unique to autonomous or controlled motivation.

This decision also has methodological implications. Because the synthesis was conducted at the

level of reported associations, raw motivation scores from different instruments were not pooled directly.

Instead, study-specific motivation indicators were incorporated through correlation-based effect sizes in

the pooled correlation matrix. This harmonization improved comparability across studies, but it may also

introduce measurement heterogeneity. In particular, combining intrinsic, extrinsic, and overall

motivation scores into one PAM construct may attenuate some effects by blending theoretically distinct

forms of regulation, or inflate others when broader scores overlap more strongly with attitudinal or

intentional measures. For this reason, the extended TPB model in the present study should be interpreted

as representing a general motivation-related extension of TPB rather than a test of specific SDT

regulations.

Within this broader framework, the proposed PAM → ATT and PAM → PBC paths are

theoretically plausible. Students with stronger motivation are more likely to evaluate participation

positively and to perceive themselves as capable of investing effort, overcoming barriers, and sustaining

engagement. These associations are consistent with SDT, which posits that when individuals experience

stronger and more self-endorsed motivation, they tend to show more adaptive cognitions and self-

regulatory processes (Ryan & Deci, 2000). Prior studies have also reported positive associations between

motivation and sport-related attitudes or perceived capability in PE and exercise contexts (Pateña &

Sanbao, 2024).

The PAM → BI and PAM → PB paths are also theoretically defensible. TPB identifies BI as the

most proximal predictor of behavior, but motivation may still be associated with both intention formation

and sustained participation because it provides the energy and regulatory basis for continued involvement.

In PE settings, students with higher motivation may be more likely to plan participation and maintain

activity over time. Existing literature similarly indicates that motivation is positively associated with

exercise intention, sport persistence, and participation behavior (Berki et al., 2020; Çağlar & Aşçı, 2010).

Nevertheless, given that most primary studies were observational and predominantly cross-sectional,

these paths should be interpreted as theoretically specified associations rather than definitive causal

effects.

The PAM → SN path requires particular caution because its directional ordering is theoretically

debatable. In classic SDT and many SDT–TPB integration frameworks, social context and perceived

normative pressure are often treated as antecedents of motivational internalization rather than outcomes

of motivation. At the same time, some empirical work has shown that individuals with stronger

motivation may report greater perceived support or stronger awareness of expectations from significant

others (Godin & Kok, 1996). In the PE context, more motivated students may be more attentive to social

cues from teachers, peers, and parents, and may therefore perceive stronger normative encouragement.

For this reason, the present study tests PAM → SN as a theoretically specified path at the level of pooled

associations, while acknowledging that reverse or reciprocal processes remain plausible and that this path

should not be interpreted in a strong causal sense.

The present model should also be positioned carefully relative to existing SDT–TPB integrations,

particularly the Trans-Contextual Model (TCM). The TCM mainly explains how motivation developed

in PE transfers across contexts to predict out-of-school physical activity over time (Kalajas-Tilga et al.,

### 2.4 The moderating effect of educational level

Educational level may moderate some relationships in the motivation-extended TPB model because

students at different developmental stages are likely to differ in autonomy, self-regulation, social

dependence, and the way they interpret physical activity experiences. In physical education contexts, K-

12 students are usually more influenced by immediate instructional arrangements, teacher guidance,

parental support, and peer expectations, whereas university students often have greater discretion over

their schedules, stronger independent decision-making capacity, and more opportunities to regulate their

own participation behavior(Hu et al., 2021). These developmental differences suggest that the strength

of some TPB-related paths may vary across educational stages.

Rather than assuming that educational level will uniformly alter the entire TPB process, the present

study expects moderation to be more likely in motivation-related belief pathways. In particular, the links

between PAM and ATT, SN, and PBC may differ across educational levels because students’ motivation

may be interpreted and translated into evaluative, normative, and control-related beliefs in different ways

at different stages of development. For younger students, motivational experiences may be more closely

embedded in external structure and interpersonal guidance, whereas older students may connect

motivation more strongly with self-reflection, personal evaluation, and perceived competence.

Educational level may therefore shape how motivation is associated with participation-related cognitions,

even if not all downstream TPB paths differ significantly across groups.

Based on this reasoning, the following hypothesis is proposed:

H13: Educational level moderates selected relationships in the motivation-extended TPB model.

### 2.5 The moderating effect of economic development level

Regional economic development may also moderate some relationships in the motivation-extended

TPB model because physical education participation does not occur under identical material and

institutional conditions across contexts. Differences in facilities, equipment, school resources, teacher

availability, extracurricular opportunities, and broader cultural support for physical activity may shape

how students form control beliefs, respond to social expectations, and translate motivation into

## 3. Research Methodology

### 3.1 Data collection

We conducted a comprehensive search in Emerald, SAGE, Taylor & Francis, Springer Link, Google

Scholar, Web of Science, and Scopus using combinations of keywords related to the theory of planned

behavior, sport, and physical education in titles, abstracts, and keywords. The search covered studies

published between January 2020 and September 2025 and was limited to English-language journal

articles.

The search initially yielded 11,609 records, of which 1,367 were duplicates. After duplicate removal,

10,242 records remained for title/abstract screening. At this stage, studies were excluded if they were not

quantitative SEM-based studies (n = 2,307), were not published in English (n = 214), or were not focused

on sport or physical education (n = 6,772). Full texts of the remaining studies were then reviewed. We

further excluded studies whose participants were not K-12 students or undergraduates (n = 816) and

studies that did not report a usable sample size or the statistics required to derive an effect size (n = 73).

The final sample comprised 60 independent studies (see Appendix A). Figure 2 presents the study

selection process.

### 3.2. Coding procedure

Two researchers independently coded the eligible studies. Inter-coder reliability was high (Cohen’s

κ = 0.836), indicating strong agreement between coders. Extracted information included author, title,

country/region, education stage, sample size, effect sizes for relevant relationships, and reliability

information for each construct pair when reported. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion, and

a third researcher adjudicated unresolved cases. To ensure that the stage-1 pooled correlation matrix for

MASEM was estimable, only relationships reported in at least three independent studies were retained.

Motivation was the only additional construct that met this criterion and was therefore retained as PAM

in the extended model. Studies with incomplete reporting were excluded when neither a usable sample

size nor sufficient statistics for effect-size conversion were available. Because the synthesis pooled

correlations rather than raw scale means, no additional standardization of motivation scores was required

before aggregation. When studies reported standardized path coefficients instead of bivariate correlations,

we converted β to r using Peterson and Brown (2005) approximation, r = 0.98β + 0.05λ, where λ = 1 for

positive β and λ = 0 for negative β. When studies reported t values, we converted t to r using r =

### 3.3. Meta-analytic correlation analysis

This study employed the random‑effects meta‑analysis method proposed by Hunter and Schmidt

(2004). It utilized the Q statistic and I² index to assess the heterogeneity of effect sizes (Borenstein et al.,

2010). In addition, we assessed the risk of publication bias, which is a systematic bias that may occur

when excluding non-significant results. To address this issue, this study introduced the fail-safe N method

of Orwin (1983) to calculate the number of unpublished zero or negative effect studies required under

each relationship to change the meta-analysis results from significant to non-significant (Hamari &

Keronen, 2017).

### 3.4. Moderator analysis

We classified the sample according to the level of education and the country's economic level to

conduct the moderator analysis. The respondents in the sample were divided into two groups: K-12

(primary and secondary school) and undergraduate. If the respondents had both K-12 and undergraduate

education, the study was recorded as Mixed and excluded from the moderator analysis. The sample was

divided into developed regions (Australia, Austria, Finland, France, Ireland, Luxembourg, the United

Kingdom, Canada, Greece, Hong Kong, Estonia, Spain, and South Korea) and developing regions

(Indonesia, Pakistan, Vietnam, Saudi Arabia and China) according to the country of the sample

respondents. Suppose the country is not clearly defined, or the study includes a mix of developed and

developing countries. In that case, it is excluded from the moderator analysis to determine whether it is

a developed or developing region.

### 3.5. Meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM)

We used a two-stage MASEM approach. In stage 1, random-effects meta-analysis was used to pool

the correlation between each pair of constructs and to build the pooled correlation matrix. In stage 2, this

matrix was analyzed in a CB-SEM framework to compare the base TPB model, the internally extended

TPB model, and the motivation-extended TPB model. Following common MASEM practice, the

harmonic mean of the pairwise sample sizes was used as the stage-2 sample size because it provides a

conservative summary when pooled correlations are based on unequal Ns. However, this approach may

still underrepresent the uncertainty contributed by smaller studies and should therefore be interpreted

with caution. To represent latent constructs, we used the mean composite reliability (CR) for each

construct to derive factor loadings and residual variances. Accordingly, measurement error was addressed

consistently at the stage-2 latent-variable level, although the stage-1 pooled matrix was not separately

disattenuated using study-specific reliabilities for every individual correlation. Because the study

synthesized pooled correlations rather than raw item-level datasets, the results should be interpreted as

model-based tests of theoretically specified associations rather than definitive causal

estimates(Alamolhoda et al., 2017).

To compare the three structural models, we evaluated standard fit indices and information criteria.

Following Montazemi and Qahri-Saremi (2015), acceptable fit was indicated by NFI, CFI, RFI, IFI, and

TLI values above 0.90 and RMSEA and SRMR values below 0.08. Comparative fit across the three

models was assessed using AIC, BCC, and ECVI, with smaller values indicating better relative fit

(Cavanaugh & Neath, 2019). For the direct paths in the final model, we report standardized coefficients,

standard errors, and 95% confidence intervals.

## 4. Results

## 5. Discussion

This study examined a motivation-extended Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) model in physical

education by integrating physical activity motivation (PAM) with the traditional TPB constructs of

attitudes (ATT), subjective norms (SN), perceived behavioral control (PBC), behavioral intention (BI),

and participation behavior (PB). Overall, the results support the value of incorporating motivation more

explicitly when TPB is applied to physical education participation. Compared with the traditional TPB

model and the internally extended TPB model, the motivation-extended model showed better statistical

fit and explained a larger proportion of variance in several endogenous constructs. However, this pattern

should be interpreted as evidence that the extended model provides broader explanatory coverage at the

level of pooled associations, rather than as proof that it is universally superior across all physical

education settings or that it directly establishes intervention effectiveness.

A central finding of the present study is that PAM was positively associated with ATT, PBC, BI, and

PB in the pooled model. This pattern is consistent with prior research suggesting that motivation is

closely related to students’ positive evaluation of participation, perceived capability to engage in physical

activity, intention formation, and subsequent involvement in sport-related behavior (Chan & Hagger,

2012; Gholidahaneh et al., 2021). In this sense, the present findings support the theoretical relevance of

integrating motivation into TPB when examining physical education participation. At the same time,

PAM was treated in this study as a broad construct because the primary literature reported different

indicators, including intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, autonomous motivation, and composite

or total motivation scores. Accordingly, the present results should be interpreted as broad motivation-

related associations rather than as effects specific to one particular motivational regulation. This issue is

important because construct mixing may have attenuated some pooled effects or inflated others,

especially where broader motivation measures overlapped more strongly with attitudinal or intentional

constructs.

The findings also suggest that TPB antecedents may operate as a more interconnected belief system

than is often assumed in simplified applications of the model. The pooled SN → ATT, SN → PBC,

and PBC → ATT associations indicate that social expectations and control beliefs may be linked not

only to intention directly, but also to how students evaluate participation and how capable they feel of

engaging in it. This interpretation is broadly consistent with earlier work showing that strong group

norms and social identification can shape both attitudes and perceived control (Terry & Hogg, 1996),

and with more recent evidence suggesting that control-related beliefs may co-occur with more favorable

evaluative judgments about behavior (Fischer & Karl, 2022). In addition, prior research has argued that

TPB constructs may be more mutually embedded than is often represented in basic path specifications

(Lopes et al., 2023). Thus, the present findings do not suggest that the classic TPB is invalid, but rather

that, in physical education contexts, the boundaries among its antecedent constructs may be more

permeable than traditionally assumed.

The PAM → SN association should be interpreted with particular caution. Although the pooled

model showed a positive association between PAM and SN, this path is theoretically more contentious

than the links from PAM to ATT or PBC. In classic SDT and many SDT-TPB integrations, subjective

norms are often treated as antecedents of internalisation rather than as outcomes of motivation. For this

reason, the present result should not be interpreted as demonstrating a one-way causal process from

motivation to normative perceptions. Instead, it is more appropriate to interpret this finding as evidence

peers, and parents in physical education settings. One plausible explanation is that more motivated

students may be more attentive to social encouragement and more likely to internalise external

expectations, whereas students who perceive stronger normative support may also report higher

motivation. This interpretation is broadly consistent with the reciprocal pattern noted in related work

(Bossert et al., 2025), but reverse or reciprocal processes remain plausible and cannot be resolved on the

basis of predominantly cross-sectional primary studies.

The moderator analysis further suggests that educational stage matters, but in a selective rather than

global way. In the present results, educational level significantly moderated the PAM → ATT, PAM →

SN, and PAM → PBC paths, whereas many other paths did not differ significantly across groups. This

pattern suggests that the way motivation is linked to evaluative, normative, and control-related beliefs

may vary between K–12 students and university students. A plausible interpretation is that younger

students’ motivation is more closely embedded in immediate instructional structure and interpersonal

cues, whereas older students tend to interpret motivation in a more self-regulated and differentiated

manner. As students mature, they may become more capable of translating motivational states into stable

evaluative beliefs and perceived competence, and they may also process normative input differently

because of greater autonomy, self-reflection, and goal regulation (Bureau et al., 2022; Leyton-Roman et

al., 2020). However, because moderation was not observed across all model paths, these developmental

differences should not be overstated. The present findings therefore support context-sensitive

interpretation rather than a broad claim that educational stage uniformly changes the entire TPB process.

Although previous health-behavior research has shown that intention-behavior consistency may increase

with age and self-regulatory maturity (Lippke et al., 2010), the current meta-analytic evidence suggests

that, in this study, educational-stage differences were more clearly expressed in the motivation-to-belief

links than in the whole model structure.

The findings also suggest that contextual socioeconomic conditions may shape the strength of some

TPB-related associations, although these patterns should be interpreted cautiously. Regional economic

development may influence the material, institutional, and cultural conditions under which motivation,

control beliefs, and participation are formed. In relatively resource-rich environments, students’

perceived control may be more readily supported by access to facilities, equipment, and stable

opportunities for activity, which may strengthen the role of control-related beliefs in participation. In less

advantaged contexts, social expectations and collective encouragement may play a relatively more

visible role in shaping participation-related intentions (Prins et al., 2010). It is also possible that favorable

economic conditions amplify the association between motivation and control-related beliefs, thereby

strengthening some indirect pathways involving PAM and PBC (Zhang et al., 2025). Even so, these

contextual patterns should not be treated as fixed laws. Rather, they indicate that the applicability and

strength of TPB-related paths are likely to depend on educational and socioeconomic environments.

alongside the substantial heterogeneity observed across many relationships. The high between-study

variability indicates that the reported path coefficients are better understood as average tendencies than

as universally stable effects across all physical education contexts. Differences in measurement tools,

sample composition, school systems, cultural expectations, and socioeconomic settings likely

contributed to this variability. Therefore, although the use of random-effects models and moderator

Taken together, the present study supports the relevance of integrating motivation into TPB when

examining physical education participation and suggests that TPB-related cognitions may be more

interconnected than commonly assumed. At the same time, these conclusions should be interpreted

cautiously because the evidence is based on pooled associations derived largely from observational and

cross-sectional studies, PAM was operationalised as a broad construct, and substantial heterogeneity was

present across many effects. The contribution of the present study therefore lies primarily in

strengthening theoretical integration, refining the explanatory structure of TPB in physical education,

and generating more focused hypotheses for future longitudinal, intervention-based, and cross-context

research, rather than in establishing definitive causal mechanisms or fixed pedagogical prescriptions.

### 5.1 Theoretical implications

The main theoretical implication is not that the motivation-extended model replaces all existing

TPB frameworks, but that motivation deserves closer integration when TPB is applied to PE. The pooled

SN → ATT, SN → PBC, and PBC → ATT associations suggest that TPB antecedents may operate

as an interconnected belief system rather than as wholly separate inputs to intention. In addition, the

PAM-related paths indicate that motivation is systematically associated with both proximal beliefs and

downstream participation.

This study also helps position the model relative to existing SDT-TPB integrations. The Trans-

Contextual Model focuses on how motivational processes in PE transfer to out-of-school physical

activity across contexts and over time, whereas the present model examines within-context association

patterns and adds internal TPB links. The present findings therefore complement, rather than supersede,

prior integrative models. Because PAM was treated as a broad construct, future work should test whether

autonomous, controlled, and composite motivation measures show different path patterns in PE. At the

same time, the high between-study heterogeneity observed in several pooled relationships suggests that

these path patterns should be interpreted as average tendencies rather than universally stable effects

across all PE contexts.

### 5.2 Theory-informed practical implications

The present findings can inform, but do not by themselves validate, intervention design. Because

PAM, ATT, and PBC were positively associated with BI and PB in the pooled model, PE practitioners

may consider strategies that are consistent with these constructs, such as autonomy-supportive instruction,

mastery-oriented feedback, and opportunities for students to experience competence. However, the

current meta-analytic evidence cannot demonstrate that any specific strategy will cause behavior change

without longitudinal or experimental testing.

Teachers and schools may therefore use the model as a heuristic rather than a prescription. For

example, PE lessons can be designed to make activity outcomes more meaningful to students, reduce

perceived barriers to participation, and create supportive peer and teacher climates. Such practices are

theoretically consistent with the paths observed in the model, but their effectiveness should be evaluated

directly in specific school settings.

Future applied work could usefully compare whether younger students benefit more from external

Likewise, schools in lower-resource settings may need to address environmental constraints before

motivational supports can be expected to translate into sustained participation. These propositions remain

hypotheses for future applied testing rather than confirmed prescriptions from the current meta-analysis.

### 5.3 Limitations and future research directions

This study has several limitations. First, the included evidence base was observational and

predominantly cross-sectional, so the directional paths tested in MASEM should not be interpreted as

proof of causality. Second, heterogeneity was very high for many pooled relationships, indicating that

the average effects likely vary across countries, educational stages, measures, and study designs. Third,

PAM was harmonized across different instruments and motivational indicators; although this made a

common pooled matrix possible, construct mixing may have attenuated some effects and inflated others.

Fourth, some effect sizes were derived by converting reported β or t statistics into correlations, which

introduces approximation error. Fifth, the stage-2 MASEM used a harmonic mean sample size and

construct-level reliability corrections, both of which are defensible but imperfect simplifications.

Future research should address these limits in several ways. First, longitudinal and experimental

studies are needed to test whether the PAM-related paths, especially PAM → SN, reflect causal,

reciprocal, or context-specific processes. Second, future meta-analyses should separate autonomous,

controlled, and composite motivation indicators whenever the number of available studies permits. Third,

intervention studies in PE could build more explicitly on SDT-informed teaching strategies. For example,

Ahmadi et al. (2023)provide a useful classification of teachers’ motivational behaviors that could be used

to design and evaluate interventions aimed at strengthening higher-quality forms of student motivation.

Fourth, future integrative models should compare within-context TPB extensions with trans-contextual

frameworks to clarify when motivation works mainly through internal belief processes and when it

transfers across settings.

## 6. Conclusions

In summary, this study re-examined TPB in PE by testing internal TPB paths and a broad

motivation-related extension using two-stage MASEM across 60 independent studies. All hypothesized

paths in the final model were statistically significant, and the motivation-extended model showed the

best comparative fit. These findings support the view that motivation is systematically associated with

TPB beliefs, intentions, and physical activity participation behavior in PE-related contexts. However, the

high between-study heterogeneity, the broad operationalization of PAM, and the observational nature of

the primary evidence mean that the results should be interpreted as support for a theoretically useful

association pattern rather than as proof of causal superiority or intervention effectiveness. The model

therefore offers a basis for more focused longitudinal, experimental, and measurement-specific research.
